 Commentary 
 The exhausting 2026 election is behind us. Now, the work of improving Idaho elections begins.
 State officials should reform campaign finance and voter registration laws, and candidates should join public forms, writes guest columnist Jean Henscheid.
 Jean Henscheid 
 November 17, 2026 4:00 am 
 Informative voting pamphlets are on display in South Hills Middle School gymnasium on Election Day in Twin Falls, Idaho, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Eakin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
 With the anticipated certification of Idaho’s general election on Nov. 24, this exhausting 2026 cycle will come to a blessed end. Before the wrap, the League of Women Voters of Idaho believes a review of lessons learned and suggestions for next steps are in order.  
 We have learned: 
 Idaho voter registration laws, policies and procedures privilege men. 
 Time is up on incumbents who refuse to meet their challengers in public forums. 
 Fallout from voter fraud lies has weighed most heavily on county election officials.  
 Life must be breathed back into the notion of nonpartisan support for voters. 
 Idaho’s obsolete campaign finance laws are harmful to voters and increasingly ignored. 
 League leaders across the state sound a clarion call to executive and legislative branch office holders: Laws, policies, and administrative procedures must change. Addressing each of the five lessons above will help reset Idaho’s electoral course. 
 Revise state edicts that unequally protect the voting rights of men over women
 Her name is Alice. At 80-something, she moved into assisted living and relinquished her driver’s license. As a life-long voter, Alice was ready in early September with a U.S. birth certificate and proof of residency to request a voter ID, register and vote in November. 
 Voting rights groups say Idaho laws from 2023 create hurdles to register and vote 
 Under Idaho’s 2023 voter identification law and the 2024 Only Citizens Will Vote Act signed by the governor, her right to vote now rested in the hands of the Idaho Division of Motor Vehicles, the voter ID issuing agency. She did not get her ID in time because she was not born male and because she accepted the norm of changing her last name upon marriage. 
 If, as a male, Alice had been married three times (the fact in her case), the birth certificate and proof of residency would have been enough for the ID to be issued. Unlike a man, Alice must prove she is a U.S. citizen and, because she followed marital customs, she must also provide all documents required for her “proof of identity trail.” This means securing three certified marriage licenses obtained from different counties over 60 years. 
 These additional documents all come with a price, both in terms of monetary cost and time. Women lacking resources to shoulder these extra burdens sometimes resign themselves to becoming non-voters as an accident of birth and marital conventions. Alice, and women of her age, rarely bucked the societal expectation that their husband’s last name would become theirs. 
 Now, to vote in Idaho, they must pay the price. 
 The fix 
 Stop referring to Idaho’s voter ID as “free.” Even for men, the documents required typically come with a cost. 
 Revise Idaho laws, policies and administrative procedures that fly in the face of the Equal Protection Clause of the 14 th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution. 
 Relatedly, revise Idaho laws, policies and administrative procedures that apply an unequal poll tax to women who must obtain documentation that men do not. 
 If decisions are made to maintain the status quo, establish a state-funded structure to support all Idahoans required to collect identity trail documentation necessary to be issued a state-issued voter ID. 
 Turn the lights back on in the court of public opinion
 For more than 30 years, Idaho Public Television and the Idaho Press Club partnered with the League to sponsor Idaho Debates , a forum for incumbents and challengers to air and compare their views before a statewide audience. 
 Where are the debates? Idaho incumbents largely forgo debates and forums this year.  
 In 2023, the refusal of incumbents to appear with their opponents doomed Idaho Debates and nearly all events like them . The fits and starts involved in inviting, scheduling, rescheduling, reinviting and, finally, going without recalcitrant candidates have exhausted nonpartisan voter education organizations and frustrated the voting public. 
 While voter guides are useful, the League knows that voters headed to the polls this November with less quality information than they had when all political candidates were willing to meet each other and the public face-to-face. Excuses incumbents give for refusal to appear with their challengers run thin and can be reduced to a single fear: “If I meet with my challenger, I run the risk of voters choosing someone else.” 
 While not as prevalent as among Republican office holders, some Democratic incumbents have chosen not to participate in some nonpartisan voter education efforts. 
 Candidates who fail to provide information to nonpartisan voter guides, for example, may believe this outreach to their constituents is unnecessary or burdensome. Proliferation of voter guides has not helped. 
 The fix 
 Political parties must partner with voter education organizations to structure public forums that meet fair, nonpartisan and high-quality standards. 
 Candidates should expect to be encouraged and trained by their political parties to engage in civil discourse with their political opponents. 
 A state-funded, printed voter guide of candidates and issues should replace the current voter pamphlet sent to every Idaho household by the Office of the Secretary of State. Candidates should expect to provide campaign information to a state voter guide that draws high quality, open-ended questions from existing nonpartisan guides. 
 Acknowledge the heavy burden carried by county election staff members resulting from voter fraud lies
 Every cause of long voting lines in Canyon County and uncounted ballots in Latah and Bannock counties may never be identified, but there is no doubt county elections staff were overly burdened with reassuring voters that this election was secure. One head of elections who was asked how voters were feeling in her county said voters were more fearful and confused this year. 
 Voters wanted their ballots to count; they worried about being stricken from voter rolls, about mailing in their absentee ballots, and about something going wrong in the counting process that would exclude their votes. Voter fraud lies, perpetuated through social media, talk radio and cable news, drained county election staff members. 
 Also, new this cycle, were more questions about which state and federal laws prohibit on-duty law enforcement officers and federal agents from congregating near polling places. 
 Poll workers were trained on Idaho Code § 18-2318 which protects the “freedom of voters to exercise their franchise without interference or intimidation and to ensure the administration of an election at any polling place is undisturbed.” Training also included discussions of 18 U.S. Code § 593 which forbids armed forces from intimidating qualified electors or interfering “in any manner” with an election officers discharge of his or her duties. 
 Yes, unprecedented turnout and lengthy ballots seem to have complicated this election. Lies upon lies about widespread voter fraud added unnecessary weight to the work. 
 The fix 
 Begin now to ask which, if any, laws, policies, and administrative procedures have been implemented that may have been an over response to now-widely acknowledged falsehoods about rampant voter fraud. Do the advantages of using the less-than-perfect Department of Homeland Security’s Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, data system, for example, outweigh the taxpayer-funded administrative costs? 
 Reinforce messages that voter privacy is paramount in Idaho and that the federal government has no role in setting the times, places and manner of state-run elections except when Congress may choose to adjust the rules. 
 Ask county officials to review support levels for county election offices to ensure they are adequate to meet demands. 
 Revive Idaho’s long-held belief in nonpartisanship
 As lies about voter fraud have seeped into our political discourse, fewer people believe that supporting voters could be a nonpartisan service. 
 This June, the U.S. League of Women Voters warned its volunteer members that the federal government was targeting nonprofits it suspected of engaging in voter fraud. That month, without warning, federal agents stormed the offices of one Ohio nonprofit looking for such fraud. None was found. 
 In late September, LWVUS was forced to address allegations by the Kansas attorney general that League members in Leavenworth were “buying” the votes of college students. The offense? Members of that League were distributing $5 Starbucks gift cards to students walking by their voter education table. 
 Closer to home, a public complaint was lodged against one of Idaho’s local Leagues alleging that two members were engaged in electioneering. The two were involved in a private conversation at a weekly public event. After years of participation, the League’s standing invitation to that event was rescinded. Suspicions dogging nonprofit voter service organizations have not produced evidence of wrongdoing, but they have succeeded in throttling our mission-driven work. 
 The fix 
 Nonprofit voter service organizations should welcome scrutiny by political parties into the support they offer voters. Sunlight is the best disinfectant.   
 Nonprofit voter service organizations should conduct internal audits to ensure that their 501(c)3 activities follow the spirit and letter of the law. Such an audit is continuous at the Idaho League.  
 Candidates, office holders, political parties and nonprofit organizations must consider themselves partners in creating an informed electorate and act accordingly. 
 Pull campaign finance law reform to the top of the legislative agenda
 Time was, an Idaho legislative candidate could spend $2,500 to run a successful campaign. The state’s campaign finance laws were written for that time. 
 Today, tens of millions of dollars are poured into Idaho’s elections and, by law, candidates and organizations are allowed to anonymize many of their funding sources. 
 In this environment, helping voters identify sources of information and verify claims has become increasingly difficult. Producers of materials distributed in opposition to Idaho’s Reproductive Freedom and Privacy Initiative (Proposition 1) were primary in flouting the requirement that a funding source be identified. 
 Idaho’s Secretary of State Phil McGrane attributed the violations to naivete and relatively poor organization. McGrane acknowledges that many candidates in Idaho are also engaged in a campaign funding “arms race” that Idaho law is inadequate to patrol. Rank and file Idaho voters tell League members they are exhausted and confused by the rhetorical onslaught this money buys. 
 The noise increasingly serves to induce fear and to obfuscate, not to educate.  
 The fix 
 Idaho legislative leaders: Finally make good on perennial promises to update campaign finance laws. The central players in American elections are informed voters, not candidates, political parties or campaign financiers. Idaho law governing campaigns should reflect this hierarchy.  
 Conduct a serious study of the “Montana Plan” approved this month by more than 60% of voters in Idaho’s neighboring conservative state. The plan changes state code to prohibit entities incorporated in Montana from spending money to influence elections at local, state and federal levels. It reaffirms that corporations are “creatures of state law” and, as such, are subject to the state’s authority to grant or rescind their powers, including the power to spend money to influence politics. While the initiative is already facing court challenges , several other states have cued up to learn more. 
 Evidence of campaign finance violations committed during this election cycle still exists in yard signs, flyers, brochures, door knocking scripts and other materials. Where possible, violators must be identified and fined albeit at the current inadequate levels ($250 each for candidates and $2,500 each for political action committees). Additional state resources will undoubtedly be necessary to conduct this investigation. 
 The wrap
 The 2026 cycle will be remembered by many as an unending slog. Idaho voters deserve a respite but myriad issues that contributed to the slog should not await redress. This immediate task belongs to everyone who believes in equal access to the ballot and in securing the integrity of elections.
